pos.personaBrief: Ajax contested possession in opposition territory and kept the ball (StatsBomb 1972, TFT 1973 keep-ball), so ball dominance defines them rather than waiting for counters.

pro.personaBrief: Ajax built through short passing with defenders stepping forward (Blankenburg) and swift forward moves after winning the ball, but did not play long.

est.personaBrief: Kovács wanted everyone able to attack and defend regardless of position, with fluid interchange of roles and close combinations.

lar.personaBrief: Over half of box entries in the 1972 final came from crosses, with Swart and the advancing Suurbier on the right; wingers were important to the shape.

blo.personaBrief: Ajax pressed high and aggressively (60% of pressures in the opposition half), with a high line and offside trap.

mar.personaBrief: Evidence is thin: a high line with offside trap suggests spatial defending, but Neeskens closely marked Mazzola in the 1972 final.

pla.personaBrief: Kovács continued an established system and let the team play its way against all opponents, with no evidence of reactive tactics.

res.personaBrief: Attacking, audacious play even in finals (flicks, keep-ball, 1973 provocation), with enthusiasm for spectacle, though results were also won.

sis.personaBrief: Kovács subordinated the exceptional abilities of Cruyff and Keizer to the team's interests, within a collective system of stars given freedom.

jog.personaBrief: Technical dribblers (47 dribbles in the 1972 final) and players like Mühren; everyone expected to run and defend, with intensity from pressing.

bas.personaBrief: Ajax built on academy products (Rep, Krol, Neeskens-era youngsters) and a young title-winning team, with Kovács continuing the club's youth culture.

lid.personaBrief: Kovács was relaxed, tolerant of stars' excesses and one of the group, in contrast with Michels' discipline (Cruyff, emerging-europe, Telex).
